source.title: Relational reasoning and inductive bias in transformers trained on a transitive inference task
source.authors: J. Geerts; Stephanie Chan; C. Clopath; K. Stachenfeld

record.tranche_reason: The study measures previous-token and induction-head attention patterns, tracks induction strength during training, and ablates heads in a transitive-inference task. This is a conceptual test of induction-circuit formation and its relation to abrupt in-context learning, rather than an explicit reproduction of the original task and measure.
record.gate_note: The authors also report transitive-inference results for in-weights learning and for geometric prompts on LLMs. Those results do not measure induction heads or their formation; the LLM prompting results are recorded under fits_no_version. The paper cites earlier findings on induction circuits, which are not recorded as its own results.
record.test_reason: In a new setting, an adjacent-pair in-context transitive-inference task, the study measures previous-token and induction heads in a 2-layer attention-only transformer, tracks induction strength against the loss phase change, and ablates heads. It also shows that linear-regression pretraining yields no induction circuit. These are its own results on V1, V2 and V5. The task and measure differ from the original, so this is T3 rather than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add that the authors argue the ICL algorithm adapts to task demands: copying-type training yields induction heads, linear-regression pretraining does not. In LLMs, congruent (IWL-like) problems show more transitive inference than incongruent ones.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a transitive-inference task rather than the original induction-head task, defines induction strength through attention to correct versus incorrect in-context tokens, and examines head ablations and alternative pretraining regimes.
record.method_sensitivity: Training regime changes the measured circuit and generalization: adjacent-only ICL, ICL trained with non-adjacent queries, and linear-regression-pretrained ICL give different outcomes. LLM transitive-inference results also vary with geometric prompt and item condition.

fits_no_version.finding: Geometric prompts changed transitive-inference accuracy in LLMs. Number-line prompts beat circle prompts except in Gemma 1B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Geometric prompting alters LLM in-context transitive inference, especially on incongruent items.

fits_no_version.finding: Models trained via adjacent-pair ICL fail to generalize transitively, unlike IWL or linear-regression-pretrained ICL.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Induction-style match-and-copy solutions block transitive generalization in ICL.

record.problems: The mechanistic experiments use a small, simple transitive-inference task and two-layer models; the authors state that LLM internal mechanisms were not analyzed. Small-model results are from single training runs in the main experiments, although key findings are reported as replicated across 10 independent runs. Exact values for induction-strength and ablation outcomes are not stated in the text. The paper says seven LLMs in the results, while its appendix lists additional model labels.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every L2 head's plotted induction-strength value or every head-pair ablation value: the paper's prose reports these results collectively, and exact per-head values are only plotted in Figures 4B-D. No other result rows were omitted.

untested.parts: Causal composition (e.g. K-composition) between the L1 previous-token heads and the L2 induction heads; standard repeated-token copying.
Bump in the loss curve; width of the transition window; standard in-context learning score.
All: no large models analysed mechanistically.
All: one architecture; mechanistic results come from single runs. The 10-seed replication covered behaviour only, not circuits.
All: sub-steps of formation are not analysed.

missing.what: Whether induction heads form in the ICL model trained with non-adjacent queries, and in the full transformer with MLPs. The paper does not report this.

record.verdict_notes: The induction heads are used to explain a behavioural failure, not studied for themselves. The 10-seed replication covers behaviour, not circuits. Ablation values exist only in figures. Fig. 4D's caption conflicts with the text on which head is retained. Tranche changed from T2 to T3 because this is a new task setting, not a different method on the same question.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not establish that the same mechanism operates across other copying tasks or model families. The linear-regression-pretrained condition tests a different training regime.
The study reports a sharp induction-strength increase concurrent with a loss/accuracy phase change, but does not report a transient bump in training loss or quantify the width of the transition.
No measurement of induction heads as the mechanism behind most in-context learning in large transformers.
No test of induction behaviour across model families, sizes, or training runs in general, or in other architectures or modalities.
The study compares a small number of training regimes on a transitive-inference task; it does not map general data-property effects or establish how broadly induction-head formation depends on setup.
No test of the main mechanism for few-shot task learning, as distinct from the studied transitive-inference and adjacent-pair matching task.
The study does not resolve whether induction-circuit formation comprises multiple sequential sub-steps or overlapping transitions.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer trained on adjacent-pair in-context TI
rows.size_stated: 2 attention-only layers; 8 attention heads per layer
rows.operation_detail: Examined attention patterns during in-context transitive inference.
rows.measure: Presence of previous-token and induction-head attention patterns
rows.value: Previous-token heads in L1 and induction heads in L2 were observed.
rows.note: The authors describe these patterns as an induction circuit associated with the model's adjacent-pair match-and-copy strategy.
rows.check: State is fine for the presence of L1 previous-token heads and L2 induction heads. Composition between them is inferred from attention patterns, not tested.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2.1, Figure 4A–B; architecture in Appendix A.3.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer trained on adjacent-pair in-context TI
rows.size_stated: 2 attention-only layers; 8 attention heads per layer
rows.operation_detail: Tracked induction strength of L2 attention heads during training.
rows.measure: Induction strength, defined as attention to the correct in-context token minus average attention to incorrect in-context tokens
rows.value: Each L2 head showed a sharp increase in induction strength concurrent with the sudden drop in in-context learning loss.
rows.note: The text identifies the coincident loss change as occurring at 12,000 steps. Exact induction-strength values are presented only in the figure.
rows.check: Should not link V1 or V5. It measures timing: induction strength rises sharply as the ICL loss drops at ~12,000 steps. No loss bump or window width is reported.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2 identifies the phase change at 12000 steps; Section 3.2.1 and Figure 4B describe concurrent sharp increases in induction strength.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer trained on adjacent-pair in-context TI
rows.size_stated: 2 attention-only layers; 8 attention heads per layer
rows.operation_detail: Ablated L2 head 4 individually by setting its output to zero.
rows.value: Significant performance degradation; head 4 had low induction strength.
rows.note: The authors interpret head 4 as routing essential information, rather than as one of the stronger induction heads.
rows.check: Head 4 has low induction strength yet is the only head whose single ablation hurts accuracy. This shows a routing component beyond the induction heads. Value is figure-only.

source_check.correct: State: cannot_determine for V1. Removing L2 head 4 significantly degrades performance despite its low induction strength; this does not establish incomplete previous-token/induction composition. The qualitative degradation is explicitly stated in prose.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2.1, paragraph on individual L2-head ablations; Figure 4C; Appendix A.5.
source_check.problem: Head 4's causal importance does not measure whether V1's composition mechanism appears incompletely.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer trained on adjacent-pair in-context TI
rows.size_stated: 2 attention-only layers; 8 attention heads per layer
rows.operation_detail: Ablated individual L2 heads while retaining the other heads.

conditions.value: each L2 head other than head 4; outcomes summarized together in the text

rows.value: Removing any of the other heads individually had only minimal impact.
rows.note: The prose reports the other heads collectively; individual numerical values are not stated.
rows.check: Minimal impact from single-head ablation reflects redundancy among the induction heads. It cannot show whether they matter. Values are figure-only.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer trained on adjacent-pair in-context TI
rows.size_stated: 2 attention-only layers; 8 attention heads per layer
rows.operation_detail: Retained head 4 and one additional head i, ablating all other heads.

conditions.value: head 4 and one additional L2 head i

rows.measure: Accuracy on in-context prediction as a function of the retained head's induction strength
rows.value: Performance scaled directly with the induction strength of head i.
rows.note: The authors interpret head 4 as routing information and the other induction-capable heads as performing pattern matching.
rows.check: No baseline value is stated; the scaling with induction strength is shown only in Fig. 4D. Text says 'all but head i and 4' but the caption says 'head 0'.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2.1, retained-head ablation paragraph; Figure 4D heading and caption.
source_check.problem: The prose and panel heading specify retaining head 4 and head i, but the caption specifies head 0 and head i. The scaling relationship is explicitly stated in prose.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer trained on adjacent-pair in-context TI
rows.size_stated: 2 attention-only layers; 8 attention heads per layer
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated transitive generalization to non-adjacent query pairs after training on adjacent pairs only.

conditions.value: non-adjacent pairs, including internal pairs without terminal items

rows.value: No transitive inference on internal non-adjacent pairs; accuracy was at chance. Performance was above chance for some queries containing terminal items.
rows.note: The authors state that terminal-item performance does not require transitive generalization.
rows.check: Measures transitive generalization, not induction-head formation or behaviour, so it bears on no version.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer trained on in-context TI with non-adjacent queries
rows.operation_detail: Included non-adjacent query pairs during training.
rows.value: The model learned transitive generalization, with above-chance performance on internal non-adjacent pairs.
rows.note: The authors state this training regime did not produce a symbolic-distance effect.
rows.check: No induction-head measure for this training regime. Transitive generalization is not a version's construct.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer pretrained on in-context linear regression
rows.stage_stated: 50,000 iterations of linear-regression pretraining, then evaluated on TI
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed attention patterns after linear-regression pretraining.
rows.measure: Presence of an induction-circuit attention pattern
rows.baseline: standard adjacent-pair ICL model, which showed L1 previous-token and L2 induction heads
rows.value: No evidence of the induction-circuit structure; attention was diffuse across positions and heads.
rows.note: The authors attribute the model's transitive-inference behaviour to distributed representations.
rows.check: Should link V5 only: training data determined whether the induction circuit formed. Absence under a non-copying pretraining task does not challenge V1.

rows.subject: two-layer attention-only transformer pretrained on in-context linear regression
rows.stage_stated: 50,000 iterations of linear-regression pretraining, then evaluated on TI
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated transitive inference after in-context linear-regression pretraining.
rows.value: Transitive inference was observed; accuracy increased with greater symbolic distance.
rows.note: The prose describes transitive inference and a symbolic-distance effect; exact accuracies are shown in the figure.
rows.check: Transitive-inference accuracy after linear-regression pretraining is not an induction-head measure.

rows.subject: seven tested language models (aggregate as reported)
rows.operation_detail: Compared number-line and circle geometric prompts on ReCogLab transitive-inference questions.

conditions.value: aggregate result across seven models, as stated in the text

rows.value: Number-line prompts outperformed circle prompts across the tested models except Gemma 1B; the advantage was most pronounced in incongruent and permuted conditions.
rows.uncertainty: SEM shown in Figure 6; exact values not stated in the text
rows.note: This measures transitive inference under geometric prompts, not induction-head behaviour; the paper separately describes a weak reversal for Gemma 1B.
rows.check: LLM prompting result; no induction-head measure.

rows.subject: Gemma 1B
rows.operation_detail: Compared number-line and circle geometric prompts on ReCogLab transitive-inference questions.

conditions.value: geometric-prompt evaluation; specific condition values not stated

rows.measure: Transitive-inference accuracy difference between geometric prompts
rows.value: The smallest model showed a weak reversal of the usual number-line advantage.
rows.uncertainty: SEM shown in figures; exact values not stated in the text
rows.note: This result concerns prompted transitive inference, not induction-head behaviour.
rows.check: LLM prompting result; no induction-head measure.

relationships.condition: 2-layer attention-only model trained on adjacent-pair in-context TI
relationships.reason: L1 previous-token and L2 induction heads appear, and accuracy scales with the retained head's induction strength (R1, R5).
relationships.display_finding: Layer-1 previous-token heads and layer-2 induction heads appeared, with accuracy increasing alongside the retained head's induction strength.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: 2-layer attention-only model trained on adjacent-pair in-context TI
source_check.reason: R1 reports L1 previous-token and L2 induction patterns; R5 links retained-head induction strength to prediction performance. These support the mechanism in this setting, although composition itself is inferred rather than directly tested.

relationships.reason: A low-induction-strength head (head 4) is the essential one. The circuit also needs a routing head beyond the previous-token/induction pair (R3).
relationships.display_finding: Head 4 was essential despite weak induction strength, and the circuit required routing beyond the previous-token and induction heads.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R3 establishes the importance of a low-induction-strength L2 head. V1 does not assert that the previous-token/induction pair alone is sufficient, and this ablation does not show that their composition fails or is incomplete.

relationships.reason: Each L2 head's induction strength rises sharply together with the abrupt ICL loss drop at ~12,000 steps (R2).
relationships.display_finding: Each second-layer head's induction strength rose sharply alongside an abrupt ICL loss drop at approximately 12,000 steps.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: R2 reports sharp induction-strength increases concurrent with the abrupt ICL loss drop, identified at 12000 steps. A loss bump, token-index ICL measure, and transition-window width are untested.

relationships.condition: Copying-type TI training versus in-context linear-regression pretraining
relationships.reason: The induction circuit forms under adjacent-pair TI training but is absent, with diffuse attention, after linear-regression pretraining (R8).
relationships.display_finding: Adjacent-pair transitive-inference training produced an induction circuit, whereas linear-regression pretraining produced diffuse attention without that circuit.

source_check.reason: R8 and Section 4.2 explicitly contrast induction circuits under copying-type training with their absence and diffuse attention after linear-regression pretraining.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is v3, dated 11 May 2026, titled Relational reasoning and inductive bias in transformers and large language models. Its checklist states that code is on GitHub, conflicting with the pack's code=n; availability was not independently checked.

statements.correction: Two-layer attention-only TI model; retain L2 head 4 and head i according to Section 3.2.1; prediction performance scales directly with head i's induction strength; Figure 4D caption instead names head 0.
statements.problem: R5 is cited, but the statement provides no study-specific result or attribution for this paper.

statements.correction: Section 3.2.1: ablating L2 head 4 significantly degrades performance; other individual L2-head ablations have minimal impact; head 4 has low induction strength; authors suggest an information-routing role; previous-token composition is not directly tested.
statements.problem: The ablation result is accurate, but routing is an interpretation, and needing another head does not establish a limitation of V1, which does not assert that two heads alone suffice.

statements.correction: Adjacent-pair TI training produces previous-token and induction-head patterns; in-context linear-regression pretraining produces diffuse attention without evidence of that induction circuit; Sections 3.3.1 and 4.2.
